implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore is the canonical realization: acquire() blocks and takes a permit, acquire(int) takes several, tryAcquire(timeout, unit) bounds the wait, release(n) returns permits, and reducePermits(int) shrinks the bound at runtime. The constructor's fairness flag selects FIFO ordering (fair) or barging (non-fair, higher throughput); a semaphore initialised to 1 behaves as a binary semaphore and - unlike a Lock - has no notion of ownership, so a permit may be released by a different thread, which is the documented route for deadlock recovery. The classic hand-written form (synchronized + wait/notify counter) is never needed; virtual threads change nothing in the API and simply park cheaply while blocked in acquire().
pitfalls: release() is unchecked and Semaphore has no maximum: an extra or stray release raises the permit count above the constructor value, silently widening the concurrency bound.
A non-fair semaphore permits barging, so a hot producer can starve waiting threads; use fairness for resource pools and non-fair only where throughput dominates.
acquire() throws InterruptedException and clears the thread's interrupt status; swallowing it leaves a task that can no longer be cancelled.
